author: Danica Rachel
title: Operation Paperclip: The Nazis behind the US space program
content:
The Apollo moon landings are some of the most impressive technical feats ever achieved, and, for capitalism’s boosters, definitive evidence of the superiority of Western capitalism over all other social systems. The United States beating the Soviet Union to the finish line in the space race is held up as the ultimate triumph of capitalism over communism. But the path that took humans to the heavens began in the depths of hell: the Mittelbau-Dora concentration camp in Nazi Germany.

Built near the town of Nordhausen in central Germany, Mittelbau-Dora provided its prisoners as slaves to the Mittelwerk. This was a factory built under a mountain for the mass production of the V2 rocket, the world’s first long-range guided ballistic missile. The several thousand civilians killed in London and Antwerp by V2s were not the only victims of these Nazi weapons: at least 20,000 prisoners died as a result of the conditions in Mittelbau-Dora and the Mittelwerk.

Edwin Katzenellenbogen, who was convicted for crimes committed as a doctor at the Buchenwald camp, described Dora as “the Hell of all the concentration camps”. Tens of thousands of prisoners worked in interchanging 12-hour shifts, first to dig the kilometres-long tunnels of the Mittelwerk, then on the dark production lines within.

Sanitation was absent, disease and starvation were rampant, and collective punishment was common. Prisoners were hanged in groups of up to a dozen at a time, and on at least one occasion, bodies were left to dangle over the areas where others were forced to continue working.

Wernher von Braun was an SS officer, scientific director of the V-weapons project, and head of the Mittelbau-Dora planning office. He came from an aristocratic family in the German empire, and was among the first pioneers of advanced rocket science. Through the interwar years, Germany was banned from investing in many kinds of weaponry under the Treaty of Versailles, but rockets were obscure enough to avoid being on the list. During this time, von Braun became a leading designer and inventor of the engines needed to propel explosive missiles over incredible distances.

He joined the Nazi Party in 1937. If you believe his version of events, he joined only to be allowed to continue his scientific work. Regardless of his political loyalty, he was at least comfortable enough with the genocidal policies of the Third Reich to enjoy the slave labour it provided to him from Mittelbau-Dora. He was certainly aware of the reality of the Mittelwerk, having visited the tunnels himself at least ten times.

As the walls closed in on the Third Reich, with US and British forces moving in from the west and Russians from the east, von Braun hid the most important of the design documents for constructing V2s. Alongside Major General Walter Dornberger, head of the German army’s weapons department, von Braun used the hidden documents as leverage to get an amnesty with the Americans, betting that the US wanted the weapons more than they cared about prosecuting war criminals.

He was right. Von Braun, Dornberger and many other German experts in weapons of many terrifying forms—ballistic, chemical, and biological—were brought across the Atlantic under a secret program known as Operation Paperclip. They began work in the US, making weapons for a new, but no less bloodthirsty, empire. Their pasts were whitewashed, with the story being that they were innocent scientists forced by circumstance into working for the Nazi regime.

For his part, Joseph Stalin got the Mittelwerk factory itself, which continued operation for a few years before its machinery was brought back to Russia, along with thousands of German technicians needed to operate it. The USSR also got the equipment and methods to manufacture sarin gas, a chemical weapon so potent that contact with a single droplet causes a painful death.

Sarin was invented by Nazi chemists, among them Otto Ambros, who tested it on Auschwitz prisoners. Ambros was convicted for crimes against humanity in the Nuremberg trials, but that wasn’t a barrier to later working for US chemical companies and the US army. Within a few years of the end of the war, both imperial superpowers were producing large quantities of sarin and other chemical weapons.

The Cold War and the arms race 

The new phase of world imperialism had the globe divided into the West, with the US on top, against the East orbiting the USSR. The prospect of direct hot war between the empires gave way to the Cold War, and the arms race continued. Both sides had nuclear and thermonuclear bombs, the most destructive weapons ever created. The next step was to be able to use them to precisely target any location on Earth.

The idea of an intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) being fired between continents, from Europe to America or vice versa, drove weapons development in the immediate postwar years. Rocket science was central to this, and the Nazi V2 was to become the ancestor of modern rocketry.

Space exploration was tied up with the race to ICBMs from the beginning. Von Braun himself was obsessed with concepts of lunar bases and hypothetical expeditions to Mars. The launch of the Russian satellite Sputnik in October 1957, the first artificial object put into orbit, was the starter’s gun for the space race.

Sputnik really showed up the US, which had been coasting on the assumption that it was ahead. Sputnik proved that in fact the USSR was winning the race in space technology and also in ICBMs—they had used one to launch Sputnik. NASA, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, was established the next year. The US launched its own satellite in February 1958, only four months after Sputnik.

In September 1962, US President John F. Kennedy announced his government’s intention to send men to the moon in a speech at Rice University. The famous words, “we choose to go to the moon … not because [it is] easy, but because [it is] hard”, were preceded by Orwellian double-speak about how the US must “occupy a position of pre-eminence” in space to preserve “peace”. That is, the US must win this arms race so that no other empire would be able to dominate the planet. As JFK spoke, the US military was escalating its war in Vietnam.

The US would proceed to be beaten to every major milestone in the space race except for boots on the moon itself: the first artificial satellite, the first animal in space, the first human in space, and the first spacewalk were all accomplished by the USSR.

The advantage that NASA had over Moscow was von Braun and the other Nazi rocket scientists, who were the world’s leading experts. Former high-ranking Nazis were involved in every significant US development in space and rocket technology in the course of the space race.

In 1954, Bell Labs created the first guided surface-to-air missile. This was developed by Dornberger, who would go on to be vice-president of the Bell Aircraft corporation and a consultant for Boeing.

In 1958, America’s first satellite was launched on a rocket designed by von Braun. He would be the first director of the Marshall Space Flight Center, NASA’s main base of operations for rocket research.

Kurt Debus was the first director of NASA’s Launch Center. He oversaw the launches of the first US satellite, the first American in space, and all of the Apollo mission launches. He was well qualified, because overseeing launches of rockets was the job Hitler gave him as an SS officer.

And the famous Saturn V rockets that propelled the Apollo missions were developed under the management of Arthur Rudolph, former deputy head of V2 production at the Mittelwerk. Von Braun, of course, was also centrally involved.

The developments made in rocketry that were needed for the space program were the same developments needed for the US to be able to build ICBMs. The goal of landing a rocket on the moon instead of on Moscow, and delivering explorers instead of nuclear warheads, was ultimately just a gloss over what was really weapons research for the Cold War.

The Paperclip scientists did not fall into obscurity as nameless technicians. Many of them became very public leaders of the US space program, and hardcore advocates for the militarisation of space.

Von Braun in particular was a prolific writer for science magazines. A 1952 issue of the magazine 

Collier’s

, featuring articles under the heading “Man Will Conquer Space Soon”, inspired Walt Disney to get in touch with him. The Nazi rocket expert helped to design parts of Disneyland and consulted for TV specials produced by Disney. After the space race, von Braun was a consulting editor for 

Popular Science

, one of the US’s most widely-read science magazines, until his death in 1977.

The truth about von Braun and his colleagues is today widely acknowledged. But that doesn’t stop many from continuing to venerate him, with his leadership role in NASA being his main legacy. The National Space Society, a US space science non-profit, has awarded the “Wernher von Braun Memorial Award” every second year since 1993 to recognise “excellence in management of and leadership for a space-related project”. Past recipients include Elon Musk and current NASA administrator Jared Isaacman.

What is less remembered is Mittelbau-Dora and the tens of thousands of innocent lives lost there. It is a tragedy of history that the name Wernher von Braun is known more than the names of those like Jean Michel.

Resistance

Michel was an organiser in the French Resistance against Nazi occupation. He was arrested by the Gestapo in 1943 and ended up in Mittelbau-Dora, where he spent close to two years. His memoir, 

Dora

, is both horrifying in its stories of the cruelty of the Nazi regime, and one of the most inspiring tales of resistance available.

Even in the deepest darkness the spirits of Michel and other prisoners were never broken. Secret networks organised sabotage on the V2 production lines, snuck in to SS quarters to listen to British broadcasts on the radio, and spread news about the advance of the Allied armies towards Germany. They even constructed a radio transmitter they planned to use to call for help when those armies got close enough.

No telling of the story of space exploration should be considered complete without beginning with Mittelbau-Dora. Not only is it the starting point, it is also emblematic of what is at the heart of competition over space. The driving force behind Nazi rocket science was the same force behind the space races of the Cold War and today: imperial domination and all the violence that comes with it.

This September, the US confirmed publicly for the first time that it has deployed weapons into orbit around Earth. More missions to the moon are planned by today’s biggest powers, the US and China. Capitalism continues to walk down the pathway to the final frontier that began at Mittelbau-Dora, and each step brings the threat of all-out war closer.

title: Palestine supporters guilty once again, declares Murdoch press
content:

Whether it’s the shooting of fifteen people on Bondi Beach, explosives found in caravans, the looting of shops in Paris or a shocking attack on a politician with a LandCruiser, Palestine supporters cop the blame.

author: Luca Tavan
title: Europe’s youth and workers in revolt
content:
The metaphor of a tinderbox is one of the most overused in politics. But how else could you describe the situation in Europe today, where every small spark of resistance seems to be catching and turning into a powerful blaze? 

Things kicked off in France in late September, when students in the working-class suburb of Créteil in the South-east of Paris blockaded their school in protest against poor conditions. This has since grown into the deepest challenge French President Emmanuel Macron has faced in his ten years in power. On October 17, students were joined by workers in a national mobilisation of 800,000. Strikes, demonstrations, blockades and riots have all played a role in this movement. It’s not just the radical left comparing this situation to the legendary student and worker uprising of May 1968.

In Spain, anger at the eviction of María del Carmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman whose rent was raised 230 percent when her apartment was acquired by an investment firm, has generated a massive movement for housing justice. The streets have forced the centre-left Sanchez government to call early elections, and typically hesitant union leaders to schedule a general strike for November 11. 

Protests have rocked Albania since May, in response to an environmentally catastrophic luxury resort development tied to the Trump family. On October 13, youth inspired by the French protests brought their own demands over education and wages into the mix, turning the movement into a national uprising. Government buildings have been invaded and burnt, and the call for the downfall of Edi Rama’s government is widespread. It is the country’s largest revolt since the fall of Stalinist regime in the early 1990s.  

In Italy, mass protests pledging to “fare come in Francia” (to do as in France) last weekend turned into standoffs against the police. In Milan, 250 people were detained, more than 80 percent of whom were minors. Belgium, Portugal, and Ireland have seen mass protests and strikes taking aim at austerity and intolerable working conditions. 

This marks the biggest wave of protests on the continent in at least a generation. Anyone who wants to see capitalism one day toppled and replaced with a system really fit for human beings should take great hope from these events. 

There’s no telling how long these struggles will continue, whether they will lose momentum, or if massive state repression will succeed in intimidating many off the streets. But this convergence of different struggles provides a glimpse of the possibility of rebuilding class-based politics after a decade characterised by despair and far right ascendancy. 

The roots of the revolt 

While these different movements are profoundly shaped by their specific national contexts, they have common roots in decades of battered living standards and attacks on workers. An entire generation suffered the consequences of the 2008 economic crisis - wages were slashed, young people were left without the prospect of ever finding a job, and social services were gutted to bail out the banks. 

Italy provides perhaps the sharpest example of the consequences of this class war waged by the rich: according to data from Italy's Parliamentary Budget Office, private sector workers have seen their real wages fall by 6.6 percent between 1990 and 2026. 

In countries experiencing economic recovery, young people are learning that they bear the costs of boom as well as bust. New jobs created are insecure, and wage increases are offset by soaring housing costs. 

This long, bitter experience has brought questions of social class back to the fore and changed the character of struggle. A comparison of the current occupation of Madrid’s Puerta del Sol with the last one is instructive. 2011’s 

Indignados

movement shared many characteristics with the protests of today, fuelled by anger at low wages, evictions and the callousness of the political class. It was an inspiring and important moment for the left. But the politics of the movement were organically populist, seeking to build a cross-class alliance of Spanish ‘citizens’ against the political caste they blamed for the country’s ruin. The most popular slogans reflected this - like “real democracy now!” and “they don’t represent us”. 

This sentiment was also expressed in a hostility to the organised left and workers’ movement within the occupation - seen by many participants as just another facet of the “politics” they felt alienated from. Unions and left parties were even banned by the movement from participating in its marches. This tragically misguided decision put real limits on the extent to which the struggle could deepen and spread from the square to the workplaces. 

Today, the movement is consciously associated with the traditions of the left and working-class struggle. One of the most popular slogans is “Long live the struggle of the working class,”, and visitors to the occupation in Puerta del Sol are greeted with the banners of the radical left, from the anarchist CNT to the Coordinadora Juvenil Socialista (Socialist Youth). They can even take a walk down a thoroughfare protesters have named the “Paseo de Rosa Luxemburg.” 

It’s also not surprising that youth in general, and students in particular, have been the leavening agent and the detonator of so many of these struggles. Young people have been the motor behind every great movement of historical change over the history of capitalism.

Today, the lives of a new generation are being shaped by an alarming new political context - characterised not just by class attacks, but also by the reorganisation of world capitalism around rising war and authoritarianism. 

That militarism and austerity are just two sides of the same coin is clear to student protesters in France: the government is attempting to pass €54 billion in social spending cuts, while boasting that they are ahead of schedule with plans to double military spending. German students resisting the potential reintroduction of conscription have made the same connection, with chants like “The rich want war, the youth want a future” and “Our only war is the class war”. 

Ruling-class hypocrites sermonise about violence 

Much of the domestic response to these movements and international commentary has focused on rioting and alleged “violence” of some demonstrators. In a televised address over the weekend, Emmanuel Macron criticised what he called ‘unbridled violence’, asking “how could French people do this to France?”

But much of this ‘violence’ is a response to brutal state repression, a fact which warrants little attention in mainstream media coverage. In France, riots were provoked by outrageous police tactics. One 

eyewitness

 account describes: “officers patrolled in groups of four or five mopeds, each carrying a pair of armed officers. One officer stands ready to jump off, beat protesters indiscriminately and speed away before anyone can retaliate.”

The denunciation of violence is particularly ironic from the French president. Macron currently enjoys a narrower social base than many dictatorships (a recent Ipsos BVA-Cesi survey found that 82 percent disapproved of his performance) and has only been able to hold on to power through the routine and systematic use of violence. In the current wave of protests, one student has lost a hand, one an arm, another an eye. 

There has also been much establishment consternation about property damage, particularly after the burning of the historic town hall in the French town of Limonge. Karl

 

Marx wrote on this theme 150 years ago, as troops moved in to crush the Paris Commune, murdering thousands of workers: “The bourgeoisie of the whole world, which looks complacently upon the wholesale massacre after the battle, is convulsed by horror at the desecration of brick and mortar!” 

Those who rule over a system based on such brutal violence are in no position to remonstrate about the rights of buildings. 

If many of the participants in these movements are willing to defend a variety of forms of resistance, from the strike to the blockade to the riot, it’s because of an inevitable impatience that comes from learning how far you get when you go through the “proper channels.”  Anjeza Marku, an Albanian student, told the Austrian newspaper 

Der Standard

: L

“We protested peacefully for 135 days, but those in power merely insulted the participants. The public sees the youth as Albania’s last hope—we have often even been compared to the youth in France. But the government couldn’t care less whether we protest peacefully. It won’t listen to our voices anyway”.

Repression and racism 

The establishment's focus on the supposed violence of these movements has two aims. First, to criminalise resistance, and second, for a wing of the ruling class, to racialise it in public consciousness. 

The response of Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s far-right government is typical. It has sent 500 additional troops to Milan and rushed through a new “security decree” further penalising protests and allowing for 

preventive detention of minors

. 

At the same time, the government and their right-wing backers in the media have made a concerted attempt to blame the unrest on “maranza, a racist slur for groups of North African youth in working class suburbs. Deputy Premier Matteo Salvini complained the squares were filled with “maranza and rotten left-wing riff-raff.” and has threatened to strip Italian-born migrants who riot of their citizenship rights. Businessman and current Defence Minister Guido Crosetto has accused youth of waging a ‘hybrid war’ against Italian society. 

The reason migrant youth have had a prominent place in the demonstrations is obvious. Working-class migrants have to suffer the double blow of economic exploitation and racist humiliation. Moroccan youth who faced down heavily armed police in Bologna last weekend weren’t doing so for the first time. In July, the city saw its own “George Floyd'” moment, when protests erupted after police killed Abderrahim Fakir, a Moroccan migrant suffering a psychiatric episode. Migrants living in Fakir’s neighbourhood of Pilastro are used to being targeted. During 2020 regional elections, Matteo Salvini performed a stunt in the area where he rang the bell of a Tunisian family’s home to ask them over the intercom if they were drug dealers. No wonder that when resistance breaks out, people who are so beaten and repressed rush to the front lines. 

This racialised authoritarian response is being carried by the far right from Europe across the world. Trump addressed a Kansas rally on Tuesday to denounce the movement and describe France as a country “conquered, looted, and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists and communists.” Here in Australia, Pauline Hanson has warned: “Unless Australia stops importing people who reject our democracy, our way of life … these riots will eventually be coming to Australian cities”. Sky News has attempted to draw the link between the European revolt and sinister forces at home, with segments like: “Pro-Palestine rioters ‘energised’ by anti-West sentiments.” The right-wing press has hysterically denounced an upcoming student strike against Hanson on November 11, accusing the high-schoolers of planning a “France-style riot.” 

The sharp divergence of responses to this wave of revolt, described either as the great hope for a more just world or a terrifying plot to Islamicise the west, reflects the depth of the political polarisation that has been produced. But it also reflects the asymmetry of that polarisation, one in which the far right is several orders of magnitude stronger than the left and has had its conspiratorial and fascistic worldview embraced as a permanent and legitimate wing of capitalist politics. The radicalisation on the right continues to build. In Italy where Meloni’s far-right coalition is losing its lustre, it now faces a challenge in the form of the hardline fascist Futuro Nazionale, led by retired army general Roberto Vanacci.

Challenges for the left 

These hopeful struggles in Europe have emerged in a pretty bleak period. The ascendancy of the far right and multiplying horrors of capitalism are felt especially by people on the left who are aware of the long-term challenges for our side. Decades of defeat, demoralisation and working-class disorganisation have had a profound impact on the politics of the left. One reflection of this has been the tendency for socialists to lower their horizons and adapt to the politics of the centre-left, accepting Spain’s Pedro Sanchez or Brazil’s Lula da Silva as the height of their ambition. 

Another expression of this demoralisation is the retreat in some left-wing circles into doomerism and crisis-mongering, emphasising the potentially apocalyptic direction of world capitalism without an argument about how the forces to resist it could be built.

These struggles show another possibility. They are a vindication of Marxism’s central claim: that the functioning of capitalism contains within it potentially explosive contradictions, which can rapidly burst onto the scene. The capitalist system can never come good on its promises of a good life for the majority. And the potential power of the masses of people that have no real stake in this rotten order can be obscured and repressed, but it can never be eradicated. 

People are driven to act again and again. This is the only thing that can open up the possibility not just winning immediate gains but also creating ideological fissures which can lead to a break with the dominant order. Lenin reflected on this basic point after the failed revolution of 1905:

“Only struggle educates the exploited class. Only struggle discloses to it the magnitude of its own power, widens its horizon, enhances its abilities, clarifies its mind, forges its will.”

But it’s not enough to champion resistance. The challenge for socialists is not only to act as participants, but to try to give shape and direction to it and argue for a way forward. There will be many obstacles on the road to deepening these struggles, including opportunistic capitalist politicians who want to ride these movements into power, as in Albania, and conservative union leaders who only want strikes according to a neatly planned timetable, as in Spain and France.  

The last great wave of European revolt in 2011 generated exciting new possibilities. But ultimately the political forces it generated led things to disaster. In Spain, the populist party Podemos channelled resistance in a parliamentary direction and ultimately ended up in coalition with the centre-left they pledged to replace. In Greece, a party that emerged as a coalition of the radical left ended up forming a government, only to rapidly capitulate to the financial pressure of the ruling class and become as bad as the centre parties they had denounced.  

But despite the weight of so many crushing defeats, a new generation is standing up and grasping toward radical solutions to the radical problems posed by capitalism. The challenge for socialists is to grab hold of this opportunity and begin building the forces for revolution in the 21st century.

author: Dougal McNeill
title: Striking for Palestine in Aotearoa
content:
Thousands of workers at universities and polytechnics (TAFEs) across Aotearoa (New Zealand) went on strike Wednesday 21 October, rallying against poor pay offers and the increasing precarity of employment in tertiary education. This was exciting enough on its own terms. The last time we went on strike, in 2022, it was the first in decades, and felt like something new. Now tertiary workers join teachers, public servants, health workers and others who have taken action over the last two years.

Our right-wing coalition government has attacked many of our rights but, in the fightback against their assault on everything from Te Tiriti o Waitangi (the country’s founding treaty with Indigenous groups) to pay equity, we’ve seen that the long drought around industrial action in these islands has been broken by welcome and nourishing rain.

Each bargaining campaign has different priorities and, at Te Herenga Waka in Wellington, my university, one part of our campaign stands out. We went on strike for Palestine. University Workers for Palestine, a campaign group bringing together staff across the country, emerged from the anti-genocide protests since 2023 to make concrete demands of institutions here. author: Robert Narai
title: Hungary 1956: a workers’ revolution against Stalinism
content:
Seventy years ago, Hungarian workers and students rose up against a brutal dictatorship that justified itself in the language of Marxism. In its place, they built workers’ councils: organs of working-class democracy, giving future generations a chance to discover the essence of revolutionary Marxism.

My grandfather, Vendel Koroknai, often played Beethoven’s Egmont Overture on his record player and spoke fondly of its role in the 1956 revolution. The overture tells the story of Lamoral, count of Egmont, who defied Spanish tyranny under the duke of Alba. His execution sparked a broader rebellion that led to Dutch independence. For the Hungarians who heard it, the parallels were striking: the Russians as the oppressive occupiers, themselves as the Dutch seeking self-determination.

They heard it because on the evening of 23 October 1956, workers and students defeated the hated AVH, the secret police of the dictatorship that had ruled Hungary for the previous eight years, in fierce street fighting and gun battles, and took control of Magyar Radio in central Budapest. They turned it into a hub for broadcasting news, appeals, morale-boosting content and, importantly, political arguments about the way forward for their revolution. Between announcements, they played the overture over and over to lift people’s spirits and give them the resolve to fight a much better-armed enemy in the form of Russian tanks. It became the unofficial anthem of the revolution. My grandfather, who at the time was a farm labourer on the outskirts of Debrecen (Hungary’s second-largest city) and a delegate and militia leader in one of the workers’ councils, recalled: “It wasn’t just filler. It was a prophecy, articulating the hopes, dreams and aspirations of a people fighting for their liberation.”

Whether they knew it or not, Hungarian workers and students were also creating a radical alternative to both Stalinist and Western barbarism. At the height of the Cold War, they broke the so-called communist regime’s repressive arms—the secret police were dispersed, the police defected or stood aside, the army disintegrated—even as parts of its executive and bureaucratic machinery kept functioning. Into the space that opened up, they built workers’ councils, elected and recallable, running factories, farms, whole cities and towns. My grandfather was one of those workers, and it was his first taste of any political freedoms.

Stalinists who defend the bureaucratic monstrosities of the Soviet Union have always called this a counter-revolution, the work of fascists and Western agents, and used that claim to justify sending in the tanks. (The term “tankie” is derived from this argument.) The Hungarian far right, Viktor Orbán chief among them, calls it something else: a rehearsal for 1989 and the fall of the “communist” system, proto-capitalists fighting to restore private property and the free market. Neither is true. Hungarian workers were not fighting for capitalism, Stalinist or Western. The councils they built were organs of workers’ power and the basis for a democratic society run by the working class: genuine socialism and communism. This was a workers’ revolution, and the people who made it included men like my grandfather, who had lost his family’s farm to the regime that now called him a fascist.

As the American Trotskyist Hal Draper wrote at the time: “Hungary opens a new era with the first revolution against the Stalinist system.” Hungarian workers and students proved the working class could still make revolutions. They proved the so-called communist regimes were counterrevolutionary. And they cracked, for the first time on this scale, the grip Stalinism held over communist parties across the world.













PART ONE: THE OCTOBER UPRISING

Background

The Red Army occupied Hungary at the end of World War Two. With the tacit approval of the West, a Russian-backed dictatorship was installed under Mátyás Rákosi, who called himself “Stalin’s best Hungarian disciple”. Like the other Eastern European regimes established at this time, Hungary called itself a “workers’ state”. It was anything but. Workers like my grandfather had to perform backbreaking labour to meet production targets set by bureaucrats. They had no say in what was produced or how, or in any broader political decision. They were paid pitiful wages that could hardly buy bread and milk.

Peasants were driven into collective farms at gunpoint, and the hatred this produced never went away. (My grandfather’s family farm was seized in the late 1940s and he was forced to work in the coal mines of Bátonyterenye, in the north of Hungary.) Much of the Hungarian countryside became a grain colony for the Russian Empire, producing hunger, starvation and famine. Workers lived in fear of torture, imprisonment or death at the hands of the secret police, the AVH, and the system of prisons and concentration camps they ran. All opposition within the Communist Party was eliminated through regular purges. My grandfather used to say there were only three kinds of people in Hungary in those years: those in prison, those who’d just got out, and those waiting to go in.

This was Stalinism: a bureaucratic dictatorship ruling over the working class, dressed up in the language of the movement it had strangled. It was never a continuation of October 1917, when Russian workers, peasants and soldiers seized state power through soviets (the Russian word for “council”), but a complete break from it. Civil war and isolation had ruined the Russian economy and decimated the working class that made the revolution. The soviets were reduced to empty shells, and a bureaucracy stepped into the vacuum and began to develop a will of its own as the revolutionary movement ebbed. By the time it had consolidated its grip, the language of 1917 survived only as camouflage for its opposite. After 1945, this system, not the one workers had built in October 1917, was exported into Eastern Europe: bureaucratic state capitalism.

Clockwise from top left: The Stalin monument in Budapest, 1953 (Photo: Gyula Nagy); Compulsory grain deliveries in a rural village, 1951 (Photo: Fortepan); Woodworking factory hall, 1951 (Fortepan); Workers’ lodgings in the 1950s (Fortepan); Ganz Ship Repair Yard workers build a Soviet merchant vessel as part of reparations, 1940s (Fortepan).

Stalin’s death in 1953 created a crisis at the top of these regimes, since most of their authority derived from him as a figure. His replacement, Nikita Khrushchev, cynically acknowledged Stalin’s crimes in a bid to expand his own power base and present a more “liberal” face. But “de-Stalinisation” did nothing to challenge the fundamental structures of the system. Workers remained exploited and oppressed. It did, however, open space for opposition and dissent and raised expectations among certain sections of society. In Hungary, Rákosi was briefly replaced by the reformer Imre Nagy in 1953. Rákosi returned in 1955, but Moscow removed him in July 1956, replacing him with his ally Ernő Gerő, another hardliner. Nagy’s brief rule inspired hope among Hungarian workers, students and intellectuals, and his ousting was remembered with outrage. And Hungary wasn’t alone. Working-class rebellions had already broken out in East Germany in 1953 and in Poland, at Poznań, in June 1956.

Opposition circles started meeting inside the Hungarian Communist Party: the Petőfi Circle in Budapest, the Kossuth Circle in Debrecen, and the Writers’ Union. They were made up of intellectuals and students who supported Nagy and wanted reform. They were hardly radical, but they attracted new members who believed change was possible.

Workers weren’t involved in these groups. But some of their ideas, such as giving workers a greater say in how production was run, influenced some workers and intersected with the dissent already rumbling in the factories and on the farms. My grandfather recalled the climate at the time, which was reflective of the attitudes of many workers:

“We had no interest in joining any of these [official opposition groups] ... but all the talk of change and infighting at the top did start to make many of us think that this so-called monolithic party was not so monolithic after all.”

That is how the cracks began to appear. At a Budapest factory that autumn, a shop committee meeting turned into something closer to a trial. The minutes record the chairman, Horváth, defending the wage computation system against workers who no longer accepted being told to sit down and listen:

“Never before has anyone so harshly attacked the wage computation system”, roared Horváth.

“But are we right? Answer this question”, a voice interrupted.

“I am speaking now”, shouted Horváth. “When I finish, comrade, you may ask for the floor.”

“We cannot be forbidden to ask questions ... we have the right”, declared foreman Lengyel.

Small scenes like this multiplied across Budapest; in the countryside, they appeared in muted forms. In the oil fields of southern Zala, the tightening of production norms throughout 1955 met with little open protest, but plenty of “low-level sabotage, undisciplined behaviour and simple neglect”, as one party official put it. It wasn’t yet directed at the government. But it was the same thing happening in factory after factory and on farm after farm: a worker-peasant workforce that had never accepted the regime’s right to rule, and men like my grandfather, who had lost their land and spent years resenting it.

How the revolution began

My grandfather recalled:

“It was the first demonstration I had ever attended, given such things had not taken place in Hungary for my entire life. I will never forget how jubilant everyone was—something also very rare in Hungary. Everyone was distributing their political literature with their demands, talking, discussing, arguing. I did not like the Communists [reformers], but I did like what they were saying. And I also did think Nagy was one of the better guys who meant well. But here we were, out on the streets, demanding such things that seemed unthinkable just a few days earlier. How to guarantee these demands would be met?”

This was Piac, Debrecen’s main street, on 23 October 1956. It was a good question, and the reformers had no answer. It took thirteen days, and a great deal of blood, for Hungary’s workers to find one. Student meetings across the country had called the demonstrations in solidarity with the workers’ movement in Poland. At first, the regime permitted them and broadcast the details on official radio stations. “This was something completely unheard of in Hungary,” my grandfather continued:

“We did not think highly of the people organising the demonstrations. It was the chance to show some sort of opposition to the government that attracted us. But we also had some sense that in Poland workers had been demanding change and that was also something worth coming out for. Myself and some of my co-workers agreed that we would attend the demonstrations in the city after we finished work.”

Then came the radio announcement that permission had been withdrawn. “If anything”, my grandfather said, “it only steeled our resolve because we were now telling the government to go fuck themselves”. By the following morning, the regime could do nothing to stop the crowds from gathering. One intellectual close to the Petőfi Circle, Tamás Aczél, later described the shock of realising this wasn’t going to stay a debate among writers: “[I]t was then that we realised, that everybody realised, that this wasn’t just an affair of a few Communist intellectuals but that everyone felt as strongly, the same way, against the regime”. Another prominent intellectual admitted afterwards that “the idea of an uprising never entered our minds”.

At this stage, the demonstrators did not want a revolution. No one carried guns, not even stones. Members of the Communist Party led the demonstrations, carrying portraits of Lenin and Imre Nagy, and the most common demand was for Nagy to take over the government. In Budapest, the crowds gathered before the statue of Józef Bem, a Polish hero of the Hungarian revolution of 1848, where the Writers’ Union read out its demands: a more independent policy for Hungary within the Soviet bloc, factories co-run by workers and specialists, peasants free to decide whether they joined a cooperative, and Nagy reinstated as prime minister. The demonstrators sang Sándor Petőfi’s “National Song”, the revolutionary song of the 1848 uprising against the Austrian Empire (a poem my grandfather can recite by heart).













The crowds then began moving toward Parliament Square, in Debrecen as in Budapest. Nagy tried to address the crowd in Budapest, but his calls for calm and order did not match their mood. The demonstrations were drawing in people who wanted more than a few reforms. “Many of us began to shout, ‘Out with the Russians! Death to Rákosi! Free and fair elections!’”, my grandfather said. “Others shouted ‘Nagy to power!’”

Then news broke that Gerő had denounced the demonstrators as wanting to “poison Hungary and create disorder”. A section of the protest in Budapest broke off towards Magyar Radio to insist on the right to broadcast a reply. Another marched to the huge statue of Stalin in the city park and tore it down with hammers and ropes, leaving only the boots. In Debrecen, demonstrators like my grandfather were tearing the symbols of the regime from buildings and public spaces.













At Magyar Radio, massive lines of AVH blocked the building. The crowd sent a small delegation inside. Time passed with no sign of the delegates, and the crowd surged towards the police lines. First came tear gas, but the crowd was undeterred. Then came a burst of machine-gun fire.

With that single action, the revolution had begun. A few demonstrators fell. For thousands of others, the purpose of the demonstration changed: if they did not destroy their enemy, it would destroy them. They fought with stones and petrol bombs, and demonstrators serving in the armed forces called on their units to distribute arms to the crowd. Workers, who had stood on the sidelines, were drawn into the fray. Street fighting raged through the night. Barricades went up, party offices and AVH stations were burned, and hated AVH men were lynched on the streets. Russian tanks were sent in but were met block by block by small battalions of youths with petrol bombs. By the end of the night, the radio was in the hands of the insurgents, and Beethoven’s 

Egmont Overture

 was blaring out of its speakers.

The answer to my grandfather’s question was being given in Debrecen as well:

“Soldiers had refused to fire upon us when we reached the parliament building. But the AVH had opened fire and killed maybe 30 or 40 people. Those of us who weren’t already armed were given arms by the soldiers or went home to fetch their hunting rifles. We went back to our farms, factories and neighbourhoods and told our co-workers and neighbours what was happening, formed ourselves into armed units and delegations and prepared to take on the AVH. By morning, news had broken of the fighting in Budapest and the fall of the Gerő government. Delegates from all the big factories and farms, officers from the barracks, representatives of those who had led the demonstrations—we all met at the Lajos Kossuth University to discuss and decide upon a course of action. A general strike was called and within days the government had been overthrown.”

The violent suppression of peaceful demonstrators unleashed a well of bitterness fed by almost a decade of dictatorship, poverty and AVH brutality. In days, the state’s repressive apparatus, seemingly all-powerful the week before, collapsed, even as parts of its administrative machinery kept ticking over underneath. Police and soldiers handed their weapons to the insurgents. Army tanks carried Hungarian flags with the Russian insignia cut out.

A new government was declared on 24 October, led by Nagy. One decree demanded Russian troops “restore law and order” and another proclaimed martial law. This did nothing to stop the fighting. A general strike spread across the country demanding the removal of all Russian forces and that those responsible for the massacres be held to account.

The rise of the workers’ councils

The struggle against the dictatorship was not confined to armed confrontation with Russian tanks and the remnants of the AVH. By the third day of the revolution, 26 October, people everywhere were establishing institutions to express their new power. Revolutionary councils formed in the towns, the villages and the quarters of the cities, in newspaper offices and government ministries, in colleges, on collective farms and above all in the factories. The running of factories, the distribution of food and the publication of newspapers all passed from the disintegrating apparatus of the old state to the new organs of popular power. My grandfather described how this system of workers’ democracy was set up and how it functioned on his own collective farm and across the wider city of Debrecen:

“In every factory, farm, government building, army barracks, university, and school we had established these councils to respond to the massacres and determine how we would smash the AVH and the Communist regime. On our farm, instead of some stupid bureaucrat telling us what to do, we got rid of the ones we didn’t like and elected the ones who were actually helpful, alongside other workers like myself—the ones who were the most opinionated or showed the most initiative. I had authority because I’d been one of the first to take up arms, and for many, because I wasn’t a member of the Communist Party.

“We had armed detachments as well: a militia. We’d elect and re-elect roles whenever we thought it was needed, so you’d often change what you were doing depending on what needed to be done. I was a delegate to many of the initial meetings in Debrecen, then changed my role when I went to Budapest to bring food and medical supplies to the fighters. Every morning, or any time we thought it necessary, we called meetings and argued about what to do. If your colleagues didn’t like what you were saying or doing, they could call a meeting, raise their concerns, call a vote, and if you lost, have you recalled. It was the total opposite of a dictatorship. This was working-class democracy.”

In Győr, the Revolutionary Council assumed control over the whole area. Győr’s National Council was one of the most powerful bodies to emerge outside Budapest, and it had a clear leader, Attila Szigeti, who, unlike many younger delegates elsewhere, had been a political functionary under the old Communist government before the revolution. The councils drew their leadership from wherever it actually existed, including from inside the apparatus they were now overthrowing. In Miskolc, the Workers’ Council and the Student Parliament held power. In Debrecen, the Debrecen Socialist Revolutionary Committee assumed authority over the entire city.

Peter Fryer was a member of the British Communist Party and correspondent for its newspaper, 

Daily Worker

. Sent to Hungary to report on what he was told was a fascist counter-revolution, he found “a genuine workers’ revolution”. At the Győr town hall, he wrote that the committees, in their striking resemblance to the councils of Russia in 1905 and February 1917, were remarkably uniform:

“They were at once organs of insurrection—the coming together of delegates elected by factories and universities, mines and army units—and organs of popular self-government which the armed people trusted. Of course, as in every real revolution ‘from below’ there was ‘too much’ talking, arguing, bickering, coming and going, froth, excitement, agitation, ferment. That is one side of the picture. The other is the emergence to leading positions of ordinary men, women and youths, whom the AVH domination had submerged. The revolution thrust them forward, aroused their civic pride and latent genius for organisation, and set them to work to build democracy out of the ruins of bureaucracy.”













As the councils grew, the government announced more concessions to re-establish its authority, including recognising the councils themselves, in a bid to let the party machine seize control. In many instances, the plan backfired. At a telephone factory in Budapest, a worker who had spent 25 October fighting in the streets went back the next day to find 800 of his 3,000 colleagues gathered in the factory hall, listening to management try to get ahead of what was coming. The SZOT, the National Trade Union Council, had appealed for workers’ councils to be constituted so workers would have a say in the factory.

The workers interpreted the appeal differently from how the SZOT and party headquarters expected—they took it seriously. They proceeded to elect workers, their own representatives, to the council and not the men suggested by the leadership. Nineteen or twenty of the 25 council members were workers rather than staff, roughly half in their twenties, radicalised by the previous two days’ fighting. The director asked to stay on, but only as an ordinary toolmaker, the job he’d had before his promotion, and the workers let him.

Recognition was meant to bring the councils under the party’s control. Instead, it gave the youngest and most militant workers official sanction for what they were already doing, and they came to dominate the councils rather than the party officials.

The better-organised councils sent delegations to see the ministers and press their demands. My grandfather joined one of these delegations to bring food and medical supplies to Budapest and to press the central government for its demands. Across the councils, he related, the tone of their statements was always the same: “We will give our full support to the new government ... when the new government accepts our programme, particularly the withdrawal of Russian troops”.

The central government had two choices: crush the revolution mercilessly, using enormous numbers of Russian troops and tanks, or make huge concessions to the insurgents. The government and party leaders chose the second. Nagy appeared on a broadcast, saying most insurgents were not counter-revolutionaries, and promised to withdraw Russian troops from Budapest immediately. By the night of 31 October, no Russian units were seen in any major city. Nagy also announced a new government that abolished the one-party system and said the workers’ councils and local councils would be officially recognised. The revolution, it seemed, had been successful.

PART TWO: AN UNFINISHED REVOLUTION

The significance of the workers’ councils

By the end of October, my grandfather sat on a council on his own farm and took part in meetings of the Debrecen Socialist Revolutionary Committee. Yet the dominant view on the left in both the West and East at the time would have branded him, and everyone around him, a counter-revolutionary.

The crudest explanation of what took place was that the events in Hungary were a “counter-revolution” led by fascists and Western agents. But the people who challenged the party leadership throughout 1956 and led the 23 October demonstrations were often dedicated members of the Hungarian Communist Party. As for the events that followed, there are accounts of individual fascists trying to take control, and there is no doubt the West tried to spin the events for its own purposes, but this was hardly the main dynamic. Peter Fryer was sent to Hungary for the sole purpose of reporting on this “fascist counter-revolution” and instead found a genuine workers’ revolution.

Other commentators accepted that this might be true. Although the motives of those involved were honourable, just and certainly not fascist, they were, in practice, weakening the state and preparing the ground for counter-revolution, for “a restoration of capitalism”. This is wrong on many counts. It implies that workers who had taken control of their own factories through workers’ councils would for some reason hand them back to private capitalists. (Try telling the delegates on my grandfather’s collective farm that their reward was returning the old landlords they equally despised.) It implies that peasants freed from forced grain requisitioning would give their land back to the pre-war landowners. Anyone who knows the history of the peasantry knows they will resist all attempts, from whatever quarter, to take their land away. As for the workers, those who believe workers at the height of a revolution need a police guard to stop them from handing their factories over to capitalists have no faith in workers’ ability to run the world. That is why so many of the same manifestoes that demanded free elections and the withdrawal of Russian troops also declared: we do not want a return to the pre-war landowners, nor the factories handed to the capitalists, nor the mines to the barons, nor our armies to the fascist enemies of the people.

Instead, workers pointed to an alternative: a form of social organisation superior to either Rákosi’s bureaucratic state capitalism or the West’s monopoly state capitalism, one based on workers’ control from below and on production for human need, not profit or competition. In building it, they rediscovered, without any of the history to guide them, the tradition of the councils of 1905 and 1917, and they challenged the ruling classes of East and West alike.

A meeting of the workers’ council at Stalinvarosz steel plant, Dunapentele.

Class forces

To understand why the councils took the shape they did, it helps to see who stood where. Before 1956, three major classes existed in Hungary: the workers, the peasants and the central political bureaucracy, which controlled the means of production and forced workers to sell their labour power to it, and peasants to sell their produce. My grandfather came from the peasantry and was forced into the working class. At the top of the bureaucracy sat an inner group that made decisions for the bureaucracy as a whole, comparable to the executive directors of a capitalist firm, except that it concentrated not only economic decisions but also control over the police and the use of military power.

At the top, Nagy wanted to carry out reforms because he thought that was the best way to serve the bureaucracy’s interests, while Rákosi and Gerő wanted to maintain the old way. Behind Nagy stood the Petőfi and Kossuth circles, who viewed his reform programme as a way to improve their own situation without shaking things up too much. They wanted to “reduce tension”, “restrain the movement”, “ensure its peaceful character”, not to make a social revolution. These may have been people my grandfather had stood beside in Piac. But they answered my grandfather’s question by putting Nagy in power and leaving decision-making up to them.

The popular insurgency from below looked very different. The workers’ councils were spontaneously formed bodies whose composition and programmes reflected the manner of their formation. Many of their spokespeople were old social-democratic and trade-union militants, some of whom had been imprisoned under the pre-war Horthy dictatorship or under Rákosi. Others, because of their youth, had no political background at all. This was particularly true of the factories in the big working-class areas of Csepel, Újpest and Pécs, Miskolc and Dunapentele.

On the collective farm where my grandfather worked on the outskirts of Debrecen, young workers like him dominated the council: newly proletarianised youth from the countryside with none of the traditions of the workers’ movement.

At the telephone factory referenced earlier, the older workers thought the young should take the lead: if they had been good enough to start such a glorious fight, they were good enough to represent the factory. Around 90 percent of that council belonged to the party, but the workers trusted them because they had always stood up for them, and only men with clean hands were elected.

In the council debates, you can see how Stalinism distorted and inverted everything. Those who spoke in Marxist jargon were often the most conservative rather than the most militant and class conscious. Many of the best and most militant workers rejected the standard terminology of socialist revolution and fiercely opposed the Communist Party. For workers like my grandfather, that terminology had associations with Rákosi, or even Nagy, and with the red flags that had flown over the AVH buildings and the gulags in which their communities and families were tortured or disappeared.

“Who in their right mind would identify with the same red flags flying over the AVH buildings and concentration camps that jailed and tortured our people?”, my grandfather would often remark. Workers often spoke of socialism rather than communism. Some meant reforms like those in Poland. Others were trying to reach something that existed in the heyday of the Russian Revolution of 1917, without being aware of any of its history and lessons, because they had been buried under the weight of Stalinism. And yet their slogan, “the factories and farms are ours”, summed up the essence of revolutionary Marxism.

A worker makes a political argument in a meeting of the council at Stalinvarosz steel plant, Dunapentele.

Dual power

In every great social revolution, the state apparatus that represents and maintains the old ruling class collapses. Each revolutionary class must create its own organs of power as it remoulds society in its own interests. This situation of dual power is precisely what occurred in Hungary. On one side was the Nagy government, which at least officially ruled. It controlled the ministry buildings in Budapest and was recognised by other states. Yet it had lost the capacity to enforce anything. The army had disintegrated. The AVH had fled like rats into holes. Everywhere in the neighbourhoods and provinces, on the streets, in the factories and on the farms, it was the new revolutionary councils that could get things done. My grandfather summed up the situation across the country: “A factory or farm has to work? Ask the council. Food is to be obtained? Ask the council. Medical supplies? Ask the council. Drunk and disorderly behaviour? Ask the council”.

Despite often being identified with the revolution, the Nagy government was a counter-revolutionary institution. Its first act was to declare martial law and call in Russian tanks. After that failed, and the machinery of repression collapsed, it used Nagy’s prestige as a reformer to salvage its legitimacy. The strategy of the hardline Stalinists like Gerő, brute repression, had clearly failed. Now it was time to try softer Stalinists like Nagy.

Imre Nagy speaks at a parliamentary session, with Mátyás Rákosi sitting next to him, 21 October 1954.

This highlights a second contradiction that characterises every revolution: the same people engaged in the most revolutionary acts continue to bend the knee to the old ideas. Workers like my grandfather could simultaneously think the Stalinist system had to be destroyed, serve as delegates in the workers’ councils and lead a militia, and yet think Nagy was, in his own words, “one of the better guys who meant well”, without understanding that the councils themselves could become the basis for a new type of state power. The instinct driving them, “the factories are ours”, arrived without the political scaffolding to explain what it implied: that a council running a factory today could become the foundation of a working-class government running the country tomorrow.

It was my grandfather’s question from Piac, asked on a national scale: how to guarantee these demands would be met? Who would control the factories and make the economic decisions? Who would control the state? A national system of delegated workers’ councils or the central bureaucracy? Such questions were unlikely to be asked, let alone answered, in a few days. In Russia in 1917, the workers’ and soldiers’ councils took eight months to answer them. Hungarian workers were given less than two weeks. Nagy made the final concession on 1 November, when he proclaimed Hungarian neutrality and announced his intention to leave the Warsaw Pact. On 3 November, the Russians invited the Hungarian government to send a delegation to negotiate the terms of a full withdrawal. Colonel Pál Maléter led the military delegation in the talks, which seemed to proceed satisfactorily through the afternoon and evening. Late that night, while Budapest slept, Russian secret police officers interrupted the discussions, arrested the Hungarian delegation and hauled them away to prison.

PART THREE: THE SECOND SOVIET INVASION

Counter-revolution

“I awoke on Sunday 4 November, just like everyone in Budapest, to the sound of artillery fire on the outskirts of the city”, recalled my grandfather, who had been part of a delegation that had travelled to the city a few days earlier. Russian tanks were pouring in, concentrating around the insurgent strongholds, the Kilián Barracks and the Corvin cinema, which they shelled mercilessly. Nagy spoke on the radio, saying the country was being invaded by Russia in an attempt to overthrow the government. No one yet knew the military delegation had been arrested.

Someone inside the Kilián Barracks that morning, close enough to Maléter to hear both sides of the call, recorded what happened when the colonel tried to stop the assault. The minister’s reply was far from encouraging: “I am sorry, comrade colonel. I am in no position to interfere with the Soviet military operations”, read the transcription of the conversation. Maléter’s expression hardened: “In that case, sir, I report that I shall open fire on the first Soviet tank that comes within range of the Kilián barracks”.

Colonel Pal Maleter in a meeting with Freedom Fighters. Photo: John Sadovy.

Nagy and his ministers fled to the Yugoslav embassy for sanctuary. János Kádár, a former member of Nagy’s government, reappeared after several days of absence at the head of a new government installed and backed entirely by Russian tanks. But if Nagy’s reform government quickly collapsed, the popular resistance had not.

The Hungarian people fought back with rifles and pistols, the occasional light machine gun, and above all with Molotov cocktails (petrol bombs). Workers in the industrial centres led the resistance: Csepel, Újpest, Pécs, Miskolc and, above all, Dunapentele. My grandfather, who had gone to Budapest with food and medical supplies for the fighters, was trapped there, and joined the armed resistance organised through the Corvin cinema, one of the last strongholds to fall. His account of the street fighting gives some idea of the bravery of young workers in the face of the fury unleashed on them:

“Our units usually consisted of one senior fighter, such as myself, with some form of rifle, pistol or, if you were lucky, a machine gun. Then there were the younger ones, often fifteen or sixteen, but sometimes much younger, who were smaller and more agile, and who would try and sneak up on tanks with Molotov cocktails and lob them into their cabins ... The tanks would begin shelling early in the morning when everyone was asleep in a neighbourhood to catch them by surprise. And they would carry on well into the night. Whole apartment blocks would be raised, collapsing in on their inhabitants without any warning. Those attempting to flee or surrender would be gunned down by machine-gun fire ... I will never forget the screams of boys and girls, some as young as twelve years old, as they were gunned down and in many instances blown to pieces regardless of whether they had been freedom fighters or not.”

Wittner followed the same path, leaving for Austria, returning, being arrested and sentenced to death. But her sentence was reduced to life imprisonment and she was released in 1970.
