The same savagery that put down the Paris Commune in 1871 now played out on the streets of Budapest. The Kremlin did not dare let its troops take on their opponents rifle by rifle. They could have been open to the strange ideas that had taken hold of the workers of Hungary, and might have joined them. Instead, any chance of fraternisation was sealed by tanks that, block by block, reduced whole areas of working-class districts to rubble. Between 20,00 and 30,000 people were killed in the space of a few days. Appeals went out to the US and the West for assistance. But the Western powers knew that the idea for which the freedom fighters were dying, a society ruled neither by capitalists nor by bureaucrats, democratically run from below by workers’ councils, was as dangerous to monopoly capitalist rule as to its state capitalist rival.

Photos by Michael Rougier show death and destruction on the streets of Budapest after the second Russian invasion.

The second period of dual power

Russian tanks might have crushed the armed resistance and installed Kádár’s new government, but they still did not control the Hungarian working class. Although workers could no longer take to the streets, they showed no signs of returning to work. Here began one of the most prolonged and most solid general strikes in working-class history. Industrial production stopped, electricity failed, food was in short supply, and the telephone network and the post office worked only when their workers wanted them to.

Yet life had to continue. The Kádár government could not do it, and so the task fell to the workers’ councils. Over the next few days, Kádár’s tone slid from hope to request to threat to something close to pleading, and none of it moved anyone. The strike held. People went in only to collect their pay, then walked straight back out. His own broadcast on 4 November had promised workers’ management “on the basis of the broadest democracy” in every factory. He didn’t mean it, but the promises tell you what he thought he had to say to be heard at all. Delegations kept pressing. Workers from the Ganz Electrical Works told Kádár that discussions a fortnight earlier had produced assurances, but no steps, and delegates from the 11th District’s factories drew up eight demands, more developed than anything in the first days of the revolution: collective ownership of the factories under the councils as sole directors, and a militia answerable to the councils, not the police.

On 12 November in Újpest, the town hall’s old Stalinist council tried to meet under the protection of Soviet tanks parked outside; the revolutionary council that had displaced them during the uprising turned up to the same meeting. Here, delegates from every Budapest factory were called to meet and form a Central Workers’ Council.

They met at the Egyesült Izzó lightbulb factory on 13 and 14 November, not the town hall, which police and Soviet troops had occupied overnight. Nobody controlled the door. There were no ushers, no formal chair keeping order. By one account, it was close to disorder, and the disorder was the point: this was a body answering to a crowd, not managing one. The newly constituted Greater Budapest Central Workers’ Council began work at the Transport Union headquarters and immediately became the central focus for workers across the capital.

Two things stood out about who was in the room. First, age: roughly half the delegates were in their twenties, workers who’d grown up entirely within the system they were now trying to overthrow. The second was the older layer sitting alongside them, men like Sándor Bali, veterans of the pre-war Metalworkers’ Union, some jailed under Horthy, some under Rákosi, carrying trade union traditions the younger delegates had never had the chance to inherit. It was the same mixture my grandfather had known on his farm, on a bigger stage. The delegates confronted one major problem. Despite the general strike, the workers lacked the power to enforce the demands they had stood for before 4 November. The position of the Belojannis electrical works was adopted: “We do not officially recognise the Kádár government, but we are ready to negotiate with them because, whether we recognise them or not, they are the de facto masters of the country”. Yet Kádár was unprepared to confront the councils. The Council was an institution he had never encountered: one genuinely subject to democracy from below. It could not be easily contained or corrupted.

By mid-November, the Central Workers’ Council was a national counterpower to Kádár’s government. It had a mandate from delegates elected across every major industry in the capital, complete control over whether the country’s economy functioned at all, and a government that could not physically compel anyone back to work. Kádár could not run the country without it.

But the Council could not take power from him either. The working class had been militarily defeated. The insurgent strongholds had fallen, the arms were gone, and facing the workers was an occupying army that had already shown, on 4 November, exactly what it was prepared to do. Armed insurrection against it was out of the question. It was not a lack of courage that stopped the councils from taking power. The time to do that had been before the second invasion, in the first period of dual power.

So it became a standoff. The strike could stop the country but could not remove Kádár. Kádár’s tanks could hold the streets but could not restart the factories. And the longer it lasted, the more it favoured the side with the tanks, because workers could not live on strike indefinitely.

The dissolution of the councils

The Council’s leaders argued for a tactical retreat: call off the strike in exchange for concessions, because the alternative was a strike that would collapse from hunger and take the councils’ authority down with it. The Council agreed on 16 November to return to work on the condition that negotiations actually begin. They didn’t. With every new day, Kádár took another step toward creating a new state apparatus. Two powers cannot coexist for long. Some of the Council’s leaders may have thought they could coexist, under protest, with Kádár, but Kádár knew he could not coexist with them.

On 6 December, authorities attempted to arrest two of the Council’s leaders, Sándor Rácz and Sándor Bali, at work. Only their fellow workers’ physical resistance at the Belojannis factory kept them free. On 11 December, 30 days after its birth, the first real workers’ council seen in Europe for nearly 40 years, the Central Workers’ Council of Greater Budapest, was arrested in its entirety. The workers responded with another general strike. A dozen more factories struck in protest at the arrests. At Csepel, workers staged a sit-down. Yet for all their bravery and heroism, the Hungarian working class was defeated and forced back to work. On 6 January, the Csepel Workers’ Council dissolved itself, declaring:

“Events have prevented us from fulfilling our mandate. We have no other role than to carry out government orders. We cannot carry out orders that oppose our mandate ... It is our opinion that our continued existence would help to deceive our members. We therefore return our mandate to the workers.”

By April the deputy premier, Antal Apró, was justifying the formal dissolution of the other councils on the grounds that “their composition was wholly unsuitable”. It took the regime the better part of six months to finish off what the tanks were supposed to have settled in a single Sunday morning in November. To the party bureaucrats, the workers’ councils were a nightmare that reminded them of everything they feared most. For many Hungarian workers, the councils remained a powerful symbol of what they really wanted.

Photos by Michael Rougier, left to right: Burying the dead; A reaction to carnage in the streets of Budapest; Graves of freedom fighters lie in the same cemetery with the Russian dead but are covered with offerings of flowers and wreaths.

Why did the revolution fail? Could it have won?

The most common answer is that Hungary was isolated and simply outgunned by Russian tanks. That is true to an extent, but it lets a more important failure off the hook. The revolution was persistently limited and constrained by the Nagy government, which never broke decisively with the bureaucracy it came from, tried continually to restrain the movement it was nominally leading, and ultimately laid the basis for the crushing military defeat at the hands of the second Russian invasion. If workers had taken power into their own hands, the military resistance could have become centralised and coordinated rather than the heroic, yet totally haphazard and inadequate, resistance that took place.

During the second period of dual power, just such a body did exist. The Central Workers’ Council of Greater Budapest was, in its structure and authority, comparable to the Petrograd Soviet of 1917. But it emerged too late, after the working class had been militarily defeated. The insurrection that might have changed the outcome needed to happen in the first period of dual power, before 4 November. Why was there no national counterpower created in those days? The deeper reason is the absence of a revolutionary party that could bring together the best and most leading elements of the working class.

The Bolsheviks had spent three decades building such a party. In Hungary, Stalinism’s disastrous legacy disoriented the best elements of the class. The most militant and class-conscious workers were either members of the Communist Party and didn’t understand the need to break from it, or, like my grandfather, totally hostile to the Communist Party and to political parties in general. If such a party had existed, the insurrections in Győr, Miskolc and Debrecen could have been replicated in the national capital. A genuine workers’ state in the middle of the Eastern bloc would have opened the possibility of further workers’ revolutions in both East and West, and changed the dynamics of the Cold War.

Conclusion: 70 years on

The Hungarian revolutionaries were defeated, but in defeat they did not lose everything. The meaning of the revolution lives in what it proved. The myth that the Stalinist monolith could not be shaken was shattered for a minority of radicals. Workers could lead a revolution and establish institutions, workers’ councils, that pointed to a different type of society. And what those people reached for, the moment the old order could no longer stop them, wasn’t a rush to the market or a swing to the right. It was councils, run by and answerable only to themselves. That is the answer both to the Stalinists who claimed the revolution was counterrevolutionary, and to the right-wingers who try to claim it for their own. It also demonstrated that workers’ councils alone are not enough. Without a revolutionary party capable of giving coherent political direction to the most militant and class-conscious sections of the working class, even the most heroic revolutionary movement can be defeated.

The shockwaves reached well past Hungary’s borders. Mass resignations swept through Communist Parties across the world as members who had defended the Soviet Union could no longer stomach what had been done in its name. A new anti-Stalinist left began to emerge from the wreckage.

As the reconstituted AVH hunted down militants after the defeat, my grandfather was given shelter by working-class leaders in Csepel. Knowing that, if captured, he would almost certainly be jailed and executed, he fled Hungary and spent almost a year in a camp in Austria before arriving in Australia in 1957, where, as the opening of this piece describes, the Stalinist slander about the revolution was waiting for him. He was barred from work in the Communist Party-controlled metal trades and labelled a “fascist” and “counter-revolutionary” for his association with the uprising.

I didn’t fully understand the significance of any of this as a kid, though it wasn’t for lack of exposure. My grandfather subjected me to Beethoven, tried to make me recite Hungarian poetry, and kept me up late at night telling these stories on a fairly regular basis, whether I wanted to hear them or not. I absorbed it all without grasping what it meant. Only when I became more political did I understand its significance.

He never identified as a Marxist or a communist. Stalinism had poisoned those words for him. And yet his actions, and those of the Hungarian working class in October and November 1956, were central to my own discovery of what Marxism actually means: not bureaucratic tyranny justified in the language of socialism, but the self-emancipation of the working class. The overture that was played over and over on Magyar Radio, and the poems he carried in his head, were how that meaning survived: Beethoven’s music about a man who died defying tyranny, and Petőfi’s song in which a people swears it will be slaves no longer. Despite their ultimate defeat, the Hungarian workers helped generations rediscover genuine Marxism.

author: Tom Bramble
title: US imperialism in the 21st century
content:
At the start of this century, US imperialism was at its peak. It had been a decade since its chief adversary, the Soviet Union, had crumbled; the country was now the unchallenged global superpower. Washington was bringing countries into the North Atlantic Treaty Organization that had been the USSR’s satellites in Europe, and it could rely on its allies to extend US influence into every corner of the world.

The US dominated the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund and was the most powerful nation in the United Nations. Its economy was booming, and the federal government ran surpluses. US multinationals found new markets and investment outlets worldwide. It was the heyday of “globalisation”. The US ruling class boasted that the country was a beacon to the world. As Democratic candidate Al Gore put it in one of the presidential debates in 2000:

“It is a great tribute to our founders that 224 years later this nation is now looked to by the peoples on every other continent and the peoples from every part of this Earth as a kind of model for what their future could be … The power of example is America’s greatest power in the world.”

Twenty-five years later, US rulers are not so assured. The country has suffered a series of crises, and the global balance of power has shifted. The US remains the world’s leading power, but it is wracked by dysfunction on a series of fronts. Its allies are increasingly estranged. Wars in the Middle East have exposed its diminished military power. Its tech sector and banks still lead, but its industrial base is now much weaker. Its political system is seen not as a model for what to do, but what to avoid. 

The decay of US power can be understood as the result of four interrelated phenomena: an imperial crisis in the Middle East, an economic crisis that crashed the world, the challenge from China and a political crisis that reflects and exacerbates these three trends.

The imperial crisis

The 9/11 attack on the World Trade Center in 2001 was a devastating blow to America’s sense of invulnerability. But US strategists also recognised the attack as an opportunity to advance US power—justification for a new round of wars that would intimidate the country’s rivals and allies alike and overcome the Vietnam-era legacy of widespread domestic opposition to far-flung and lengthy land wars. 

The idea of an aggressive revival of US military interventionism had been germinating in the ranks of the Republican Party for some years in its “neoconservative” wing. The leading think tank was the Project for a New American Century, founded by William Kristol and Robert Kagan. Its supporters and associates included Dick Cheney, Donald Rumsfeld, Paul Wolfowitz and John Bolton, all of whom held senior positions in the George W. Bush administration, which had won the 2000 election. 

The October 2001 invasion of Afghanistan was the first step in this wider project. Bush’s cabinet believed that the US would topple the ruling Taliban in Kabul and then lead a triumphal march through the capitals of its defeated enemies. Iraq, Iran and Syria were the main targets and, further afield, North Korea. Regime change was the objective.

In the short term, the invasion of Afghanistan was a stunning success. The Taliban were overthrown within two months. Domestic support for the war was overwhelming. It seemed US imperialism was back. Next was Iraq. The Bush administration justified its invasion by associating the country’s president, Saddam Hussein, with the 9/11 attacks and claiming that he had built an arsenal of weapons of mass destruction to threaten the West. On 19 March 2003, the US and its allies invaded Iraq. Within three weeks, US forces had taken Baghdad, and on 1 May Bush appeared on the deck of the 

USS Abraham Lincoln

 to declare “mission accomplished”. 

Yet things turned bad for the US in both countries. In Iraq, local resistance to the occupation soon emerged. By the following year, it was raging. The US responded by flattening whole neighbourhoods, deploying white phosphorus and uranium-tipped weapons. Regular sweeps of suspected resistance activists terrified neighbourhoods and filled the jails. The US destroyed civilian infrastructure providing clean water, power and health care. And it sacked more than 100,000 government employees, creating mass unemployment and impoverishing millions. The death toll rose steadily. A study by the 

Lancet

 journal in 2006 estimated 655,000 excess deaths in Iraq in the first three years of the war. Anger towards the US ran white-hot. 

The US now turned to classic colonial divide-and-rule tactics, stoking sectarian conflict on religious lines. Tens of thousands of Iraqis died in a civil war the US occupation had provoked. Actual terrorist groups now began to grow in Iraq, including the group that became the Islamic State. The Bush administration dispatched 20,000 more US troops supposedly to quell internal conflict while promoting collaborators. 

It was all to no avail. Hatred of the occupation meant the US never “pacified” Iraq. In 2009, Britain pulled its troops out, and the US followed in 2011. In 2014, the Obama administration sent troops back into Iraq to fight the Islamic State, but this was a rearguard operation. The US was eventually forced to shut its last base down on 30 September this year. American hubris had given way to humiliation.

In Afghanistan, the US occupation also ran into the sand. The US propped up a corrupt government in Kabul that depended on warlords. Resistance soon appeared. In 2009, Democratic President Barack Obama ordered a 100,000-troop surge. The Taliban gradually regained territory based on popular hatred towards the predatory US-backed government. With war weariness widespread at home, the Trump administration in 2020 negotiated a withdrawal with the Taliban to take effect in 2021. Once the US withdrew air support and contractors left, the Afghan army collapsed in a matter of days, and the Taliban took power once again.

Bush’s dream of a victory parade through the region, a springboard for US global revival, had ground to a halt. At home, the cost of two decades of war and occupation—7,000 military personnel dead, US$3 trillion spent by the Pentagon and on care for veterans and interest payments on war borrowing—killed off any patriotic surge or any notion that the Vietnam Syndrome could be finally buried. For many American victims of domestic repression, the attacks on civil liberties and anti-Muslim racism spawned by the “War on Terror” could be added to the total cost.

Such was popular revulsion at home that the next Republican to win the presidency after Bush, Donald Trump, won support in 2016 by pretending to be against war.

The US’s war on Iran this year has only added to US military failures in the Middle East. Iran was one undisputed beneficiary of US defeats in Iraq and Afghanistan, extending its influence on a range of fronts. The Trump administration, egged on by Israel, believed that years of sanctions, serious reversals among its allies and massive internal opposition had sufficiently weakened the government that a combined attack would quickly break the Islamist regime. 

But the US has failed in Iran so far. Trump’s regular proclamations of imminent victory are now treated as a joke. Despite not having landed a single Marine in Iran, the US armed forces are running out of munitions. The generals tell Trump the war is unwinnable. Arab allies see that US promises of protection have amounted to nothing. The operation is also stoking inflation in the US. The US is spending hundreds of billions of dollars on a war with no path to victory. The US military has demonstrated that it can pulverise humans and essential infrastructure but cannot extract strategic gains from its bloody wars.

Economic crisis

For all the boasting about America’s economic power at the turn of the century, the US soon suffered two heavy blows. The first was the dot-com bust. The explosion of US tech corporations in Silicon Valley in the 1990s was held up by boosters of American capitalism as vindication of the country’s strength. The Nasdaq stock market index tracking the industry rose fivefold from 1996 to its March 2000 peak. 

But by October 2002, the Nasdaq had lost more than three-quarters of its value, dragged down by rising interest rates, doubts that the dot-com businesses would ever show a profit and an end to the supply of easy venture capital. Major businesses collapsed under heavy debt. Enron, an energy trading business and among the country’s largest companies, went bust. The media, which had praised these companies for years, were now forced to expose their corrupt dealings. Tens of thousands of workers lost their jobs, while most executives cashed out and walked away scot-free. 

The global financial crisis of 2008–09 was even more severe. It started in the US housing industry, then spread to the US stock and credit markets, triggering the biggest economic bust since the Great Depression of the 1930s. In eighteen months, trillions of dollars of wealth were destroyed. Household-name banks went under. The crisis dragged down the entire global economy. Whole regions of world capitalism teetered on the brink of collapse. 

Of course, the suffering was not shared equally. The working class was shafted with job losses, wage cuts, evictions and savage austerity. Unemployment did not fall back to its pre-crisis level until 2016. Many corporations, however, received enormous government subsidies and cheap loans. The recovery was slow by historical standards, GDP rising by just 2 percent annually over the decade that followed. The US economy has never recovered the production lost during this period.

The US is currently faring relatively well compared to other advanced economies: a huge investment boom is under way, centred on tech companies, unemployment has fallen and corporate and household debt are down. But weaknesses lie beneath the surface, and the scars of the ten-year crisis are still visible. 

Federal debt has grown over the years as the government responded to the dot-com bust, the financial crisis and the pandemic by throwing trillions of dollars in subsidies to the capitalists. Successive tax cuts to corporations and the wealthy have added to the debt, as has spending on wars and war preparations. The federal government is now running budget deficits of 6 percent of GDP, unprecedented outside deep crises.

The successive crises encouraged the US central bank to keep interest rates low. This contributed to a long bull market in equities that benefited wealthy investors and exacerbated already high inequality. Since 2022, however, the Federal Reserve has raised interest rates sharply. This has not yet burst the stock market bubble, but it has increased interest payments on government debt and on companies now feverishly borrowing to invest in AI infrastructure. Annual federal interest payments now stand at nearly $1 trillion, the second-largest item on the government’s books after Social Security. Rising bond yields in turn drive up interest rates on home loans and consumer debt, hitting working-class living standards. The US economy may not be in crisis yet, but the fault lines are obvious.

The China shock

The China shock added to US troubles. At the time of Bush’s inauguration, the US regarded China as a potential rival but not a serious threat. China’s GDP was just one-eighth the size of America’s, and it had little ability to project power beyond its shores. Far from a threat, US imperialism saw China’s rise as an opportunity. Washington calculated that US capitalists could use China as a low-wage manufacturing platform and market and, on that basis, sponsored China’s entry into the World Trade Organisation in 2001.

US plans in China soon came unstuck. China grew rapidly; by 2011, its economy was half the size of the US’s. China adopted US methods and techniques to develop its own capitalist enterprises, which soon challenged the US in its domestic and export markets. China began to exert a magnetic pull on its trading partners, which increasingly looked to it for new economic opportunities.

In response, the Obama administration announced a “pivot to Asia” in 2012. Sixty percent of US naval power was to be directed to East Asia and the Pacific, and the Middle East was downgraded as the main theatre for US imperialism. In 2017, the incoming Trump administration ratcheted up the US offensive against China. Trade policies are always a weapon. Previous presidents had promoted “free trade” to advance US interests. Trump argued that this had only enriched China at the US’s expense; a high tariff wall was the only way to “Make America Great Again”. 

In the alternating Trump-Biden-Trump presidencies, different economic and diplomatic strategies have been pursued, but the common theme has been the desire to hold China at bay. These attempts have failed. China’s GDP is now two-thirds of US GDP. It produces 30 percent of global manufacturing, nearly double the US share. China now dominates global production across a range of high-tech and advanced manufacturing; its universities lead the world in science and tech research; and Chinese labs are catching up to the US’s expensive AI frontier models despite the US’s strenuous efforts to block them. 

Crucially for US imperialism, Chinese industrial capacity is powering a growing military presence that reaches hundreds of kilometres from its shores. China now has more ships than the US Navy, and its shipyards can build them much faster. US attempts to “reshore” manufacturing for military purposes have had extremely limited success. 

The Chinese ruling class now believes that it can go toe to toe with the US. The latter’s relative decline and its failed wars in the Middle East have also encouraged Russia to test US resolve in Ukraine. The turn-of-the-century unipolar moment has given way to a multipolar world. All talk of a “new American century” has receded.

Political paralysis

Imperialist failure abroad, the failures of American capitalism at home, and the China shock have shaken American politics. At the turn of the century, more than 40 percent of respondents to Gallup polling said that they had “a great deal” or “quite a lot” of confidence in US institutions. Today, the figure is just above a quarter. On the left, young people in particular were drawn to anti-capitalist politics, fuelling the Bernie Sanders surge in 2015. But most of the radicalisation has been expressed on the right. The ruling class proved incapable of stopping Donald Trump’s rise; he transformed the Republicans into a party of radical disruption and chaos. 

It speaks volumes about the state of official politics that the federal government of the world’s most important imperial power is run by con artists, grifters and anti-science nutters. Trump is attacking America’s traditional allies, one of the country’s major sources of strength, antagonising the military and foreign policy establishment, and blatantly using executive power to go after his critics and reward fealty. His budget policies are unashamedly pro-billionaire, but many of his economic policies appear little more than thought bubbles. 

Trump’s tariffs and the broader program of economic nationalism do, however, have one important goal for US imperialism: to unwind the offshoring of US manufacturing and rebuild production at home, preparing for war with China. That has been a consistent theme of both Trump’s and Biden’s terms in office. Trade and economic policy are now squarely aimed at winning the competition between the superpowers. The problem for US imperialism is that Trump’s administration is so chaotic and unpredictable, and the manufacturing base so degraded, that it may be very difficult for it to be rebuilt, short of actual war breaking out when the Pentagon will simply take over the industrial base, as it did in World War Two.

In the immediate aftermath of 9/11, Bush’s rhetoric focused on the need for the country to stand as one against a common enemy. For the Trump administration, the enemy is at home—critics of the administration and progressives more generally. Any idea of “national consensus” has gone, except perhaps in one area: Trump has the lowest favourability rating of any president since polling began.

The US may still be the world’s number-one imperial power, but compared to the turn of the century, it has declined and appears less confident and more divided. The ruling class has no strategy to stop China’s ongoing economic rise, or to lift the living standards of its own working class. It seems incapable of providing a credible narrative justifying its own economic excesses or its ongoing and obscene levels of military spending. 

But that doesn’t mean the story is over. This is a wounded beast, and wounded beasts can lash out in many directions.

author: Ben Hillier
title: ‘Post-truth’ politics is business as usual
content:
Since Donald Trump’s arrival on the scene more than a decade ago, lying in politics has become ever more shameless. It’s the “post-truth politics” era, apparently. Oxford Dictionaries, which crowned “post-truth” the word of the year when Trump first took up residence at the White House, noted that “it describes not just particular assertions, but a general characteristic of our age”. The 

Economist

 wrote at the time:

“His brazenness is not punished, but taken as evidence of his willingness to stand up to elite power … [Post-truth politics] picks out the heart of what is new: that truth is not falsified, or contested, but of secondary importance. Feelings, not facts, are what matter in this sort of campaigning.”

Yet if “post-truth” is characterised by emotional appeals and relegating facts to the sidelines, it’s not clear that politics has fundamentally changed at all.

On a 2008 autumn night in Grant Park, Chicago, Democratic president-elect Barack Obama, promoted as an articulate Harvard Law graduate with a firm grasp on reality, addressed an enormous crowd. title: Repressive one day, strike-breaking the next: Queensland workers under attack
content:
As if the right to strike hasn’t been curtailed enough. On 14 October, the Queensland Liberal National Party government accepted a raft of recommendations from a review into the state’s industrial relations laws. Restricting the right to strike is central to the changes the LNP plan to implement, including giving the industrial relations minister sweeping new powers to stop workers from taking protected industrial action. 

Under the proposed amendments, protected industrial action can be terminated by the minister “if it would ... cause significant damage to the state’s economy”. The same goes for action that would “significantly disrupt the delivery of a public service”—a direct attack on the ability of schoolteachers, paramedics, hospital workers and others to take protected action. According to industrial law firm Maurice Blackburn, the laws will also restrict the window in which protected industrial action can be taken and give employers the right to dock workers’ pay even in cases where they are still performing some duties while on strike.

The proposed amendments also target any action taken in the lead up to, or during, events such as the Brisbane Olympic games, where the minister simply needs to be satisfied that such action has “a significant effect that is contrary to the public interest” to have the power to terminate protected action.

title: Hate campaign against Andrews indicates right-wing can’t tolerate even tepid social democracy
content:
Rapturous applause swept One Nation’s campaign launch in Melbourne on 3 October as Mark Nicholson, the party’s lead candidate for the Northern Metropolitan region in the upcoming state election, declared that a One Nation government would jail former Labor premiers Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan “by Christmas”.

This was not just some one-off Trumpian gesture. Visceral hostility to Andrews, denounced by Murdoch’s 

Herald Sun

 and 

Sky News

 as “Dictator Dan”, has for years been a core feature of far-right politics.

Andrews is seen as the devil incarnate, the epitome of a communist leader akin to North Korea’s Kim Jong-Un. He is portrayed as being engaged in a dark “globalist” conspiracy to destroy the Australian way of life, including by giving a treaty to Aboriginal people and destroying important freedoms like the right to spread disease so beloved by anti-vax cookers, White Australia supporters and purveyors of Great Replacement-style conspiracy theories.

author: Luca Tavan
title: How the Socialist Party is different from the other parties
content:
Members of the Socialist Party are often asked what makes us different from other parties. Prospective left-wing voters bruised by the long history of politicians selling out their principles want to know how we will avoid becoming part of the same establishment we want to challenge. On the other hand, some left-wing Greens question whether the Socialist Party is even necessary, seeing as their party already offers similar policies. 

The only way to answer these questions properly is to explain how the Socialist Party is unlike any other in Australian politics. We have a vision of society and a political strategy that differs fundamentally from all pro-capitalist parties, from the Liberals to the Greens. So what’s so distinctive about our project? 

Socialism!

The first thing is in the name. We are a socialist party, avowedly opposed to the whole capitalist system. Of course, the meaning of the term “socialism” is contested. Many progressive politicians, from UK Greens’ Zack Polanski to New York’s Zohran Mamdani, have ridden a wave of hostility toward right-wing billionaires and use the term “socialism” to describe their goal of reformed capitalism.

author: Mary Ellen Murphy
title: Hospital doctors strike for wages, safe hours and public health
content:
In July, Victorian public hospital doctors voted 97 percent in favour of taking industrial action for the first time in 20 years. The reason is simple: the healthcare system is unsafe for patients and staff.

The Victorian healthcare system is in crisis. Systemic failures at every level compound one another. Limited access to primary care and community services leaves people more unwell and reliant on emergency departments for care. This results in long wait times, overcrowding and unsafe workloads.

Bed shortages, often caused by delays in discharging patients due to the lack of support services, are also an issue. For example, recent data from the Victorian Health Department shows that nineteen of 21 mental health units fail to admit acutely unwell patients from the emergency department within eight hours. This results in staff attempting to care for patients in under-resourced and unsuitable environments where they are at greater risk of violence. The lack of suitable facilities for mental health patients and adequate staffing also contributes to the ongoing failures to meet goals for the reduction in use of restrictive interventions such as seclusion and restraint.

author: Barry York
title: From student activism to Pentridge and beyond: the life of Barry York
content:
Barry York was a leading student radical at La Trobe University at the height of the movement against the Vietnam War. In 1972, along with two other student activists, Barry was arrested and held in Pentridge Prison for his anti-war activity. He recently self-published a memoir of his time in Pentridge as a political prisoner which will soon be available at Red Flag books.

The La Trobe struggle was part of the wider student movement opposing the Vietnam War, conscription and apartheid in the late 1960s and early 1970s. On campus, we challenged the university’s ties to political and economic power, including Chancellor Sir Archibald Glenn’s association with ICI (Imperial Chemical Industries, renamed Orica Limited in 1998), which had contracts with the government linked to the Vietnam War. ICI’s parent company also had links to the munitions and chemicals industries in apartheid South Africa. We opposed La Trobe’s rule barring students suspended elsewhere from enrolling, and questioned its possible cooperation with the Joint Intelligence Organisation. At the heart of these campaigns was a basic question: whose interests should a university serve?

“Students saying ‘good girl’ to teachers.”

“Less respect for female staff vs male in behaviour—even with the same approaches they instantly listen to males more. More inappropriate jokes—racism, homophobic and sexist jokes with little consequences. Visible [and] audible dismissal/rejection of female staff to their faces when they appear to take classes.” 

These are quotes from a Monash University report which has cast light on the disturbing sexist conditions faced by teachers and students in primary and secondary schools across the country. 

Duty of Care: Teachers’ experiences of sexism, misogyny and sexual harassment in Australian schools

 is based on the testimony of 2,600 educators and reveals the breadth and depth of the crisis. 

A common theme in the report is the lack of respect male students show female teachers. This includes frequent interrupting, ignoring of instructions, mocking and mimicking, speaking disrespectfully and refusing to accept responsibility when challenged about inappropriate behaviour. Physical aggression and intimidation were also reported, along with threats of more serious physical and sexual assault. Male students frequently make “derogatory comments toward females focusing on appearance and worth”, “jokes about gender roles e.g. the kitchen”, “inappropriate sexualised remarks about female bodies, including specifically about peers and/or staff” and “[making] sexual noises in the classroom” while female staff are trying to teach.

This behaviour is contributing to the burn-out of teachers in a profession already facing shortages due to poor pay and unmanageable workloads. One respondent put it clearly: “Being the front line and bearing the brunt of misogyny is exhausting and erodes self-worth”. According to the report, 77 percent of teachers say that sexism and misogyny have a “negative” or “very negative” impact on their wellbeing, and more than 50 percent of female teachers report that they either “occasionally” or “frequently” consider leaving the profession because of it. And the situation is getting worse—both primary and secondary teachers reported that gendered violence on the part of students had increased significantly in the previous twelve months.

Given adult teachers are feeling undermined, threatened and belittled by male students’ behaviour, the impact on teenage girls should be cause for immediate action. According to the report, “Younger students are comfortable using misogynistic language without thought e.g. calling girls in class a ‘slut’ ‘whore’ because they won’t share a highlighter”, and “Women/girls in class are okay with being treated with misogyny as this is seen as ‘normal’ now. They do not retaliate and internalise, making emotional regulation hard”. Another teacher observed: “Female students are scared to speak out and express their opinions in class with males who chastise them. I am noticing students are very hesitant to participate in discussion these days whereas it used to be female students being quite eager to share ideas and answer questions. Female students appear angrier than in the past as well”.

Male students direct sexist and misogynistic language towards their female peers freely, entrenching a toxic gender divide among students. Again, the statistics bear this out, with 80 percent of respondents agreeing that the behaviour is having a negative impact on student wellbeing. In observing and being victim to male students’ sexism—including constantly disrupting learning and making spaces hostile—girls are being socialised to accept dehumanising language and treatment and to make themselves small targets by withdrawing and accommodating to the selfish and anti-social behaviour of boys. 

And though there are undoubtedly some who are willing to challenge their peers’ appalling behaviour, it is an unacceptable environment for female students to be expected to navigate every day, while at the same time trying to do the actual tasks of deciphering Shakespeare or learning calculus. It is well established that students learn best when they feel safe, supported and respected. This is currently not the case for female students at Australian schools. 

Misogyny and the rise of the ‘manosphere’

Further evidence of the problem of sexism among male students is the frequent cases of particularly egregious behaviour that make the news. Student from 

Scots College

 and 

St Gregory’s College

 in Sydney, for example, are currently facing court for a series of alleged crimes including sexual assault, rape and common assault for two separate incidents in July and August. 

An independent cultural review of St Kevin’s College

 in 2021 confirmed that sexist and misogynistic behaviour and views were “still clearly an issue” at the school. It was commissioned following an incident in 2019 when St Kevins students horrified the public with their 

misogynistic chants on a Melbourne tram.

 In 2020, a scavenger hunt organised by students at the Shore School, one of Sydney’s most elite institutions, was 

leaked

 

and found to contain activities such as “Get with an Asian chick”, “Play porn out loud on public transport” and “Get with a chick which is 3/10 or lower (photo of the chick + the dirty work)”. And in 2024, 

male students at Yarra Valley Grammar

 were suspended when their rating system of female students was discovered. 

As many respondents to the Monash University survey noted, an important driving force of this sexism is the rise of the online “manosphere”. This consists of the open use of misogynistic language, the revival and confident reiteration of conservative gender-stereotypes, the glorification of aggressive and violent masculinity and the dehumanisation and objectification of women. It is readily accessible through various online channels, with algorithms actively targeting boys and young men. More than 87 percent of teachers noted the influence of these ideas on the boys they teach, with one describing how they have to be careful “when discussing issues regarding female contribution to society or feminist ideas so as not to provoke students to make manosphere style commentary”. Many say they face “hostile attitudes toward discussions of women’s rights and social equity” from male students, who deny systemic issues of gender inequality, question the relevance of discussing these topics, and approach them with defensiveness and aggression rather than empathy, curiosity or an openness to learning.

These sexist and misogynistic ideas resonate with boys and young men not just because they offer a sense of power and superiority in a world where feelings of powerless and inadequate are endemic. But also because they are reinforced and validated by the wider organisation of society. 

Women’s oppression under capitalism 

Well before the manosphere existed, capitalism was systematically denigrating women and their contribution to society. Women’s work and intellectual and creative contributions to society is and has long been devalued and belittled. Women are concentrated in low-status jobs and are paid less on every measure in comparison with men. They are dehumanised and objectified in pop culture, advertising and pornography, with their bodies used as props to sell things, often on the basis of making women feel they are ugly, unwanted impositions on the world unless they fix themselves with diet, cosmetics, medication, surgeries. And that they only have value insofar as they are appealing to men. Women’s wants, needs, questions and ideas are a side show in much of public and private life—in the workplace, within their families and relationships, and in popular culture. 

Women exist to be judged, policed, made the butt of jokes, dismissed, controlled and purchased. In this context, it is no wonder young people are susceptible to the extreme sexism and misogyny that is now available to them online. 

The fact that sexism in schools and society is on the rise is connected to an interesting and challenging fact of the situation; views on gender and gendered behaviour are going backward by many measures at the same time that there is an increase in curriculum content to educate children about sexual and romantic relationships, consent, stereotypes, and the reality of the sexual and domestic violence epidemic. This gap between intention and reality highlights the limitation of education programs in the absence of addressing the structural, social and economic roots of women’s oppression. 

This is also why it is not just young people who hold sexist views. A Melbourne University report, 

Misogyny, Online Radicalisation, and Youth Extremism in Australia

 which asked 1,122 young people aged 13 to 17 and 2,307 adults about their views on gender, sex and sexual relationships found similar issues across age groups. For example, about 31 percent of males from each generation surveyed (Gen Z, Gen X, Millennials, Boomers) agreed with the statement: “Attempts to give equal opportunities to women in Australia have gone too far”. A quarter of both Gen Z and Gen X males agreed that: “The husband is the head of the household and the wife should be obedient to him”, and more than 23 percent of Gen Z males and 20 percent of Millennial males responded positively to the statement “Sometimes women bother me just by being around”. 

The right weaponises misogyny

The response to the Monash University report has not been across the board soul-searching about how to combat this epidemic of sexism and support female educators and students forced to contend with such hostility. Rather, the right has seen it as an opportunity to attack teachers and engage in a culture war in which they identify men as the victims. 

Liberal leader Angus Taylor claimed that the Respectful Relationships Education program, which aims to facilitate discussions about respect and gender equality, as well as consent in relationships, is simply teachers “pushing an agenda”. Nationals’ troglodyte Matt Canavan agreed that the program is “anti-boy”. Breaking stereotypes in her own way by proving it's not 

only 

men who are misogynists, Pauline Hanson claimed that teachers are “brain-washing” students with these discussions about sexism, gender-roles, consent and how to navigate relationships. 

Their agenda is to demonise social movements that aim to advance the interests at those at the bottom of capitalism’s pecking order—in this case, women. If women can break free from the box they are put in, there’s no reason that other workers, refugees, migrants and others can’t question and challenge the status quo which oppresses them too. And this is not good for profit-making and strengthening the nation that facilitates it, which is the key concern of the right.

Fighting back

The conclusions of the Duty of Care report’s authors are a far cry from those of the right. Their official recommendations include reference to the pay and conditions of teachers being crucial to redressing the crisis of sexism in schools. If teachers, who are mostly women, were better paid, had better working conditions and if the profession was less denigrated by the media and politicians among others, it would certainly make it more incongruent for students to denigrate teachers in the classroom. 

Other recommendations include facilitating whole-school implementations of Respectful Relationships Education, improving work health and safety requirements in schools, and establishing avenues for compensation if they are breached. It is definitely true that the sexist and misogynistic abuse educators experience at work would not be accepted in most comparable workplaces, and educators should have the right to a safe workplace free from actual or threatened physical or sexual violence. At the moment, schools simply can not guarantee this. More funding for teachers and education support staff, smaller class sizes so complex and challenging behaviours are more manageable, funding for allied health such as social workers and psychologists would all help. More educational and critical discussions about gender and relationships in schools would also be welcome. 

However, we need to go much further. 

The misogyny in schools is an echo of the misogyny that characterises the rest of society, and is being normalised by the far right that is gaining ground at an alarming rate. We need an organised fightback against this. We need a political movement that promotes a vision of society that is contrary to the divisive prejudices the right thrives on—that promotes the common interest between workers, the strength that comes from unity and solidarity with the oppressed, and the power that can back that up when workers stand together and take action. We need to use every instance of resistance to reassert women’s rights, fight for dignity and equality. Women will not achieve dignity and equality in schools or anywhere else as long as profit rules and people are a means to an end. We need a socialist vision and a socialist movement that can offer something completely different.

Ridah is a public school teacher in Victoria

author: April Holcombe
title: Chinese youth in a very shit time of their lives
content:
Certain quarters of the internet are filling with content lauding contemporary China as an advanced, anti-imperialist, even socialist society. Its unrivalled high-speed rail network and its continued use of Communist jargon have encouraged some disillusioned Western youth to declare themselves in “a very Chinese time of my life”.

State-of-the-art infrastructure and Communist iconography have obvious appeal to a section of people living in decaying, imperialist and increasingly far-right-controlled Western capitalism. But there is a big difference between Instagram China, a Potemkin country showcased by influencers at the invitation of the tourism bureau and marketed to disillusioned Western youth, and the real China, a nuclear superpower ruled by bureaucrat-businessmen.  

Young Chinese people on social media—students, workers and the unemployed—use a very different kind of language than influencers do. Theirs is the language of alienation, exploitation and oppression in a society every bit as capitalist as our own.

author: Priya T.
title: Eugene Debs—the socialist who won a million votes
content:
Eugene Debs was the most popular and beloved socialist leader in United States history. Famed for exceptional speechmaking, the Socialist Party of America raised $20,000 to buy a train for Debs’ inaugural run for president in 1906. The “Red Special” carried Debs across the country to hundreds of meetings, from the union halls of mining towns to a mass gathering of more than 10,000 workers at New York’s Madison Square Garden. 

A lifetime of struggle, and the lessons born from bitter defeats, transformed Debs from a trade unionist and Democrat to a socialist committed to building a working-class party. 

Debs was born in 1855 in the small town of Terre Haute in Indiana. At fourteen, he started working on the railroads. Railways were central to the industrial expansion going on in the United States at the time, connecting major cities and transporting commodities between them. Capitalists employed gangster violence against unions, keeping working conditions dangerous and wages pitiful. Ray Ginger, in his famous 1949 biography of Debs, writes that in his fifth year on the railways, a friend and workmate of Debs fell under a train and died. Worried he’d meet the same all-too-common fate, Debs returned to Terre Haute shortly afterwards.

author: Connor Knight
title: When Australian socialists dared to dream
content:
In the years after World War One, the Australian socialist movement reached its peak influence. Socialists led big strikes, gave speeches to crowds of tens of thousands and oversaw a flourishing radical press. Thousands of workers believed socialism was possible. But until now, few historians have given this generation of Australian socialists the acknowledgement they deserve. 

Duncan Hart has been a prominent socialist in Brisbane for nearly two decades. 

His new book

, 

From Revolutionary Hopes to Shattered Dreams: The Socialist Movement in Australia:1918-1925,

 brings this momentous period of Australian socialism to life—its revolutionary promise, the fierce debates that animated it and its eventual decline. He spoke to 

Red Flag

’s Connor Knight in Brisbane about the book. 

What inspired you to write this book? 

I was inspired at first by reading some of the history on the period that did already exist. I started to get the sense that it was a much more significant period than it has been given credit for. I was inspired by reading about the people in the movement—they were genuine socialists who wanted to overthrow capitalism, not supporters of dictatorships or advocates of gradual reform.

title: Housing protests lead to general strike in Spain
content:
“I haven’t managed to defend my house, but I have tried so that others can learn how to defend theirs.” These were the words of an 87-year-old Madrid woman, Maricarmen, who posted a video from her hospital bed after Spanish authorities evicted her from the apartment she had lived in for the past 71 years. In the video, she promoted an upcoming protest at Madrid’s Plaza del Sol “so that we can eliminate this problem once and for all”.

Her eviction sparked a fire across the Spanish state. Within days, protesters had set up an encampment in the Plaza del Sol, famously the site of mass anti-austerity protests in 2011. They quickly spread to dozens of other cities, along with mass protests. A few days later came the first victory of the movement, when the vulture fund that had bought Maricarmen’s apartment building agreed to allow her to return with a new, eight-year contract and her rent capped at 30 percent of her pension.

Jacobin

title: Mega Anthropic data centre to blight Queensland
content:
Queensland is set to become home to Australia’s largest AI data centre. Last month, Liberal National Party Premier David Crisafulli announced a landmark deal with Anthropic to develop the Western Downs Digital Park, near the town of Dalby, about 250 kilometres northwest of Brisbane. Led by Singaporean developer Zerra DC, the site will be constructed in four phases, with the first building expected to be operational next year.

The data centre will occupy 725.5 hectares, an area twice the size of New York’s Central Park. Its estimated value is $32 billion, nearly five times the 2032 Brisbane Olympics infrastructure budget.

Data centres suck up huge amounts of power, driving up energy prices and accelerating climate change. When fully constructed, electro-mechanical engineer Dr Andreas Helwig told the ABC it would use the equivalent of 25 to 30 percent of Queensland’s total energy consumption.

The data centre will run primarily on electricity generated by coal and gas, drawn from the state’s electricity grid. Greenpeace estimates that the data centre would raise the grid’s emissions by 6.6 million tonnes, the equivalent of two million extra cars on the road.

title: Three years of Palestine solidarity
content:
In mid-October 2023, after the first major march against Israel’s attacks on Gaza, the director of the Palestine Solidarity Campaign UK, Ben Jamal, said to his staff: “We are probably going to need to be responding to this through marches until potentially Christmas”. He was wrong. The protests did not abate. As Israel’s offensive in Gaza continued, the number of actions across the world multiplied rapidly, eventually blossoming into one of the largest and most sustained antiwar movements in generations. From the world’s largest cities to the smallest hamlets, millions of voices rose in the same chant, with the same cadence: “Free, free Palestine!”

In the first months of the genocide, most were in the Middle East and North Africa and were especially frequent in Yemen, Iran, Turkey and Morocco. In several of these countries, major government or religious institutions backed the demonstrations.

content:
Gaza is a generational touchstone and the key dividing line of politics in the West. It has laid bare the lies of the society we live in. It has exposed the genocidal bloodlust of the political right. And it has tested official “progressive” liberal politics, which has so often shown itself to be utterly hollow or cowardly.

title: French high school students on the march
content:
“I like this kinda thing because it’s revolutionary”, a 16-year-old high school student told me as we stood out the front of her school in Nice at 7am on the last Wednesday in September. As we talked, students started arriving from across the city to join the blockade of the school, the Lycée Parc Imperial, the largest in the area.

Hundreds of students trickled in, and suddenly it was hard to tell where the sea of high schoolers started and ended. Some carried things to help build the barricades to stop anyone from entering the school.

I asked the 16-year-old if she knew all the students or whether they were from other schools. She pointed out a group of high schoolers who must have travelled from another school and said: “I don’t know them, but we are all comrades”.

This wasn’t the first blockade she had been part of at this school, but she said it was different to previous blockades. This time, it isn’t just one school but more than 1,000 being blockaded.

author: Jordan Humphreys
title: Germany’s far right surges
content:
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) made significant gains in several state elections across Germany in September. In Saxony-Anhalt, the party won a frightening 44 percent of the vote and fell just three seats short of forming government. Two weeks later, it won 38 percent in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, doubling its vote share from the previous election. Even in liberal, multicultural Berlin, the AfD vote went from 9 percent to 16 percent.

The results have sent political shockwaves across not just across Germany but the whole of Europe. It is no wonder why. The AfD is on the extreme wing of the broader far-right surge worldwide. Founded in 2013 as a Eurosceptic opposition to Chancellor Angela Merkel’s bailouts of the Greek government, the party has moved radically to the right over the last decade.

Today, the AfD calls for mass deportations and a strict blood-based concept of German citizenship, while opposing the right to political asylum. title: Student Union independence under threat at Sydney University
content:
The University of Sydney has announced its intention to intervene in the student union and potentially undermine democratic elections.

The announcement follows a controversy, concocted by the right-wing Murdoch media, about an election ticket contesting this year’s Students’ Representative Council election. The ticket, called Globalise the Intifada, drew hysterical condemnation from Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, federal Education Minister Jason Clare and a spokesperson for NSW Premier Chris Minns. Albanese told Sydney’s 

Daily Telegraph

 the slogan “is an absolute outrage that has no place in Australia”. 

Vice-chancellor Mark Scott and chancellor David Thodey joined the chorus of condemnation. 

In a statement released on 29 September

title: On the campaign trail with Victorian Socialists
content:
“We need Jasmine in parliament!”, called out Abdul. He runs Konjo, an Ethiopian cafe in Footscray. He’d just let us use the cafe as a backdrop for a promotional video we were making for the Victorian Socialists’ state election campaign. I’m running as the party’s candidate for the Western Metropolitan upper house region, and the cafe is adorned with a huge picture of Jasmine Duff, our candidate for Footscray. It is one of hundreds of campaign signs on front fences and on stakes in people’s front yards across the electorate. 

Since the last federal election, it feels like support for Victorian Socialists has grown. Back then, Jasmine was the candidate for the federal seat of Fraser—encompassing Footscray and suburbs to the west and south, including Yarraville, Sunshine and St Albans. At the booth I staffed, and have done for the last few election cycles, she received more than 20 percent of the vote. In Seddon, the booth at the scout hall recorded 18 percent for Jasmine.
